tool.name: ClassificationAccuracy

summary.para: Assesses the accuracy of a categorical map or model against reference (field-verified) classes: the error matrix, Cohen's Kappa with variance, Z test and confidence interval, weighted kappa, per-class conditional kappa, user's and producer's accuracies, the sensitivity/specificity family, F1, Gwet's AC1, Pontius-Millones disagreement, and the Olofsson et al. (2014) area-weighted accuracies and error-adjusted area estimates with confidence intervals. Values come from fields or are extracted from classified rasters/polygons, optionally as the majority in a circle (locational uncertainty). The report ends with a ready-to-run R snippet reproducing the analysis. A modernized port of Jenness and Wynne's classic Kappa extension, validated against R's reference packages. Works at every license level -- Esri's Compute Confusion Matrix needs Spatial Analyst or Image Analyst and reports far less.

tool.usage:
Assesses how well a categorical map or predictive model matches reality: habitat suitability classes against field surveys, a vegetation map against photo-interpreted plots, a land-cover classification against reference imagery. This is a modernized port of the classic ArcView Kappa analysis extension (Jenness and Wynne 2007, https://www.jennessent.com/arcview/kappa_stats.htm; methods primarily after Congalton and Green 1999), expanded with the estimators that today's journals expect -- and, unlike Esri's Compute Confusion Matrix (Spatial Analyst or Image Analyst required, welded to the Accuracy Assessment Points schema, no variances, intervals, tests or area estimates), it runs at every license level on any categorical pairing.
Inputs. The sample points (or table) hold the reference locations. The classification (predicted) classes and the observed (reference) classes each come from either an attribute field of the sample points or a classified dataset -- a raster, or a polygon feature class with a class field, chosen from the map's layers or browsed from disk -- extracted at each sample point. For rasters, the class field can name a raster attribute-table field (typically the class-name field), so extracted classes match a reference field that stores names rather than cell codes -- the original extension's "Data Field" column; blank uses the raw cell values. The two sides' class vocabularies must match (names to names, or codes to codes), or every sample counts as disagreement. Selections are honored; samples with NoData or nulls are dropped with a count.
Locational uncertainty. If sample coordinates carry GPS error, a point can land on the wrong cell of a correct map. The optional circle radius replaces the value-at-point with the majority value in a circle around each sample (ties go to the value at the point) -- the correction suggested by Dr. Congalton for the original extension. It applies to layer-extracted values only.
The classic statistics. The error matrix; overall accuracy with its exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) confidence interval, the no-information rate test (could you do as well by always guessing the commonest class?), and McNemar's marginal-symmetry test; per-class user's accuracy (how reliable is the map where it claims class X) and producer's accuracy (how much of the real class X did the map find); Cohen's Kappa -- agreement corrected for chance -- with its delta-method variance (Fleiss, Cohen and Everitt 1969), Z test against chance, and confidence interval, with the honest Chebyshev worst-case coverage note when normality is in doubt; per-class conditional kappa with standard errors; and the full 2x2 diagnostic family per class: sensitivity, specificity, omission and commission error, positive and negative predictive power, with weighted overall averages and the presence/absence guidance for two-class models.
The modern statistics. • Weighted kappa (Cohen 1968) for ordinal classes -- habitat suitability ranks, cover classes -- with linear or quadratic weights, so near-misses count more than gross errors. • F1 per class (the harmonic mean of user's and producer's accuracy; also the Dice coefficient) and macro-F1 -- the score the species-distribution-modeling and machine-learning literature reports -- plus per-class prevalence, detection rate, detection prevalence and balanced accuracy, so the report reads line-for-line against R's caret::confusionMatrix output. • Gwet's AC1 (Gwet 2008, https://doi.org/10.1348/000711006X126600), a chance-corrected agreement robust to the prevalence paradox that deflates kappa in imbalanced presence/absence designs. • Pontius-Millones quantity and allocation disagreement (Pontius and Millones 2011, https://doi.org/10.1080/01431161.2011.552923): how much of the error is in how much of each class versus where it was put -- the field's recommended replacement summary (see The kappa debate below). • Area-weighted estimates (check "Weight the analysis by map class proportions"): stratified overall/user's/producer's accuracies with standard errors and, the headline, error-adjusted area estimates per class with confidence intervals ("the map says 12,000 ha of aspen; the unbiased estimate is 9,400 +/- 1,100 ha"). The lineage of this option is direct. Card (1982, Photogrammetric Engineering and Remote Sensing 48:431-439, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19820041921) observed that the sample's class mix is rarely the landscape's class mix, so the raw error matrix describes the sample rather than the map -- and showed that weighting the matrix cells by each map class's landscape proportion restores unbiased map-level accuracies. The original kappa_stats extension implemented exactly that as its "weight analysis based on classification value landscape proportion" option (Jenness and Wynne 2007). Olofsson et al. (2014, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015) then matured Card's weighting into the field's good-practice standard, with one decisive reframing: read in the other direction, the same machinery is an unbiased area estimator -- the reference samples falling in each map class tell you how that class's area truly divides among the ground classes, so a small error rate in a large class can move more hectares than a large error rate in a small one, and the corrected areas come with standard errors. Map proportions come automatically from the classification (predicted) dataset (geodesic areas for polygons; latitude-corrected cell counts for geographic rasters) or can be typed in. The total mapped area is measured from the same dataset automatically -- the analyzed classes only, NoData excluded -- so the error-adjusted areas are reported in hectares without any typing; the total-area parameter is only an override, for an official map area or when the proportions themselves were typed in. • Optional bootstrap percentile confidence intervals for kappa and overall accuracy (seeded, reproducible) -- the modern answer where the normal approximation is doubtful. The replicates value is the number of resamples: each replicate redraws the full sample count with replacement from the original samples (computed as a multinomial draw over the error-matrix cells, which is exactly equivalent) and recomputes the statistics; 1,000 to 2,000 is the usual choice, with more giving smoother intervals at longer run times. "Doubtful" as a rule of thumb: fewer than roughly 100 to 200 samples in total, fewer than about 30 to 50 in any one class (Congalton and Green's design guideline is 50 per class), or an accuracy or kappa near its upper limit, where the sampling distribution is skewed at any sample size.
The kappa debate. A substantial modern literature argues against kappa as a routine accuracy measure -- most pointedly Pontius and Millones (2011, "Death to Kappa", https://doi.org/10.1080/01431161.2011.552923) and Foody (2020, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.111630). The complaints target the final summary statistic itself, not the analysis around it: kappa measures agreement beyond chance rather than accuracy, its chance baseline is a poor model of how maps actually err, and it is so sensitive to class prevalence that classifications with 95% overall accuracy can carry kappa values anywhere from slightly below zero to 0.90 (Foody's own demonstration). What the critics recommend reporting instead is exactly what this tool produces: the full error matrix, overall accuracy, per-class user's and producer's accuracies, and the area-adjusted good-practice estimates (Olofsson et al. 2014; Stehman and Foody 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.05.018) -- with McNemar's test (also in this report) as their recommended way to compare classifications evaluated on the same samples. Kappa nonetheless keeps its adherents: it anchors the standard textbook treatment (Congalton and Green) and decades of published accuracy statements that new work must be compared against, and even Foody grants it a legitimate remaining niche -- assessing agreement among multiple interpreters, which is precisely this tool's analysis-field comparison of observers. For the prevalence paradox specifically, Gwet's AC1 (also reported) is the robust alternative. In short: report the matrix and the accuracies as the critics ask, and quote kappa knowingly -- for comparability with the existing literature and for observer-agreement questions -- rather than as the sole headline figure.
Comparing analyses. An analysis field splits the samples -- per observer, per model, per year -- into separate analyses that are compared automatically: pairwise Z tests and the Fleiss (1981) common-kappa chi-square test, exactly as in the original's "Add Another Analysis" workflow. The Compare Accuracy Analyses tool does the same from typed kappa/variance pairs.
The same analysis in R. Every statistic here has a reference implementation in R, several maintained by the method authors themselves: psych::cohen.kappa (kappa and its Fleiss-Cohen-Everitt variance), caret::confusionMatrix (the per-class suite), yardstick::kap (weighted kappa), mapaccuracy::olofsson (the Olofsson estimators), diffeR (Pontius's own package for quantity/allocation), and irrCAC (Gwet's own package for AC1). This tool's algorithms are validated against all of them to close to machine precision, and every report ends with a ready-to-run R snippet with your own error matrix and strata weights already filled in -- paste it into R to confirm any number independently. When an analysis field splits the run into several analyses, the snippet carries every matrix and finishes with the same pairwise Z tests and Fleiss common-kappa test the report uses to compare them. The R examples start where the hard GIS work ends, though: extracting classes at samples, honoring selections, handling geodatabase formats, computing geodesic strata weights, and joining results back to the map for symbolization all happen here, inside the project where your map already is.
Outputs. The full formatted report in the messages and optionally as a text file; an optional per-class statistics table (accuracies, conditional kappa, the diagnostic family, F1, prevalence, detection rate and prevalence, balanced accuracy, and the area-weighted columns) ready to join and map; and an optional error-matrix table for further analysis. For ModelBuilder chains the tool also exposes three derived scalar outputs -- Kappa, its variance, and overall accuracy -- so a model can branch on accuracy thresholds, collect results across candidate models, or feed the Compare Accuracy Analyses tool directly (with an analysis field, the derived values carry the first analysis). For drawing the reference design in the first place, see the Estimate Sample Size tool, then the Random Point Generator and Select Random Records tools; for a plain contingency table without inference, see the Cross-Tab Statistics window.

param.name: in_features
param.displayname: Sample points or table (selection honored)

dialogReference.para: The reference samples: a point layer (required when classes are extracted from layers) or any table whose rows pair predicted and observed classes. A selection is honored.

param.name: predicted_field
param.displayname: Classification (predicted) data source attribute field

dialogReference.para: The attribute field from the Sample Points attribute table holding each sample's predicted class. Give either this field or the classified layer below.

param.name: predicted_layer
param.displayname: Classification (predicted) raster or polygon feature class

dialogReference.para: The classified dataset itself: a raster (cell values = classes) or polygons with a class field. Values are extracted at each sample point; this layer also supplies the map proportions for the area-weighted estimates.

param.name: predicted_class_field
param.displayname: Class field of the classification (predicted) dataset (polygon field, or raster attribute-table field; blank = cell values)

dialogReference.para: For a polygon feature class: the attribute field holding the class value (required). For a raster: optionally a raster attribute-table field -- typically the class-name field -- so the extracted classes match a reference field that stores names rather than the cell codes (the original extension's "Data Field" column). Blank uses the raw cell values.

param.name: observed_field
param.displayname: Observed (reference) data source attribute field

dialogReference.para: The attribute field from the Sample Points attribute table holding each sample's observed (field-verified, reference) class. Give either this field or the layer below.

param.name: observed_layer
param.displayname: Observed (reference) classified raster or polygon feature class

dialogReference.para: The classified raster or polygon feature class holding the reference classes, extracted at each sample point.

param.name: observed_class_field
param.displayname: Class field of the observed (reference) dataset (polygon field, or raster attribute-table field; blank = cell values)

dialogReference.para: For a polygon feature class: the attribute field holding the class value (required). For a raster: optionally a raster attribute-table field (e.g. a class-name field) so the extracted classes match the predicted side's vocabulary. Blank uses the raw cell values.

param.name: out_report
param.displayname: Output report file (optional -- the full report also prints in the messages)

dialogReference.para: A text file holding the complete report -- the error matrix, every statistic with its interval, the comparisons, and the ready-to-run R snippet. The .txt extension is added automatically if omitted.

param.name: out_class_table
param.displayname: Output per-class statistics table (optional)

dialogReference.para: One row per class (per analysis): sample counts, user's/producer's accuracies, conditional kappa with SE, sensitivity, specificity, predictive powers, F1, and -- when weighted -- the area-weighted accuracies with SEs and the error-adjusted area estimates. Join it back to your map to symbolize accuracy.

param.name: out_matrix_table
param.displayname: Output error-matrix table (optional)

dialogReference.para: The error matrix as a long table (Analysis, Predicted, Observed, Count) for further analysis or charting.

param.name: analysis_field
param.displayname: Analysis field (optional -- one analysis per value, compared automatically)

dialogReference.para: Split the samples into separate analyses -- per observer, per model, per year. Each gets its own full report block, and all are compared: pairwise Z tests plus the Fleiss common-kappa chi-square test.

param.name: circle_radius
param.displayname: Circle radius for locational uncertainty (optional -- majority value near each sample)

dialogReference.para: Optional: extract the majority class in a circle of this radius around each sample instead of the value exactly at the point -- the conservative choice when sample coordinates carry GPS error. Ties go to the value at the point. Applies to layer-extracted values only.

param.name: linear_units
param.displayname: Units for the circle radius

dialogReference.para: Meters, Kilometers, Feet or Miles.

param.name: weighting
param.displayname: Ordinal weighting for weighted kappa

dialogReference.para: For ordinal classes (suitability ranks, cover classes): add Cohen's weighted kappa, where near-misses count more than gross errors. Linear weights disagreements by rank distance; quadratic by its square (more forgiving of adjacent-rank confusion). Classes are ranked in their sorted order.

param.name: confidence
param.displayname: Confidence level (percent, 0 - 100)

dialogReference.para: The confidence level for every interval in the report (default 95).

param.name: weight_by_map
param.displayname: Weight the analysis by map class proportions

dialogReference.para: Adds the area-weighted block: Card (1982) / Olofsson et al. (2014) stratified accuracies with standard errors and the error-adjusted area estimates with confidence intervals -- the estimates current journals expect. The direct descendant of the original extension's weight analysis by landscape proportion option. That option implemented Card's (1982) weighting; Olofsson et al. (2014) later developed the same weighting into today's good-practice standard, using it to estimate each class's true area without bias. Proportions come from the classification (predicted) dataset automatically, or from the override table below.

param.name: design
param.displayname: Sampling design of the reference samples

dialogReference.para: How the reference samples were drawn -- stratified random by map class (each class sampled separately; the usual accuracy-assessment design) or simple random over the whole map. The variance formulas differ (Card 1982, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19820041921).

param.name: map_props
param.displayname: Map class proportions (optional override -- else computed from the classification dataset)

dialogReference.para: Optional: type each class's map proportion (or area -- values are normalized). When blank, proportions are computed from the classification (predicted) dataset: geodesic areas for polygons, latitude-corrected cell counts for rasters. With neither, the sample's own predicted-class proportions are used with a warning.

param.name: map_area_ha
param.displayname: Total map area in hectares (optional override -- else measured from the classification dataset)

dialogReference.para: Normally left blank: the tool measures the total mapped area automatically from the classification (predicted) dataset -- the area of the analyzed classes, NoData excluded; geodesic for polygons, cell size times count for projected rasters, authalic cell areas for geographic rasters -- and reports the error-adjusted area estimates in hectares (with standard errors and confidence intervals). Type a value only to override the measurement: an official map area, proportions typed by hand (typed proportions carry no area), or a geographic raster read through an attribute-table class field, whose counts carry no latitude.

param.name: boot_reps
param.displayname: Bootstrap replicates (optional -- adds percentile CIs for kappa and overall accuracy)

dialogReference.para: The number of bootstrap resamples used to build percentile confidence intervals for kappa and overall accuracy; leave blank to skip. Each replicate redraws the full number of samples with replacement from your original samples and recomputes the statistics; the middle 95% (or your confidence level) of the replicate values forms the interval. (Computationally this is a multinomial draw over the error-matrix cells -- exactly equivalent, because a sample's entire contribution to every statistic is which cell of the matrix it falls in.) 1,000 to 2,000 replicates is the usual choice -- more gives smoother intervals but takes longer. Most useful when the normal approximation behind the standard intervals is doubtful -- as a rule of thumb: fewer than roughly 100 to 200 samples in total, fewer than about 30 to 50 samples in any one class (Congalton and Green's design guideline is 50 per class), or an accuracy or kappa near its upper limit, where the sampling distribution is skewed at any sample size. The random seed below makes the intervals reproducible.

param.name: random_seed
param.displayname: Random seed (bootstrap)

dialogReference.para: Optional: the same seed reproduces the same bootstrap intervals exactly.

scriptExample.title: Classification Accuracy example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Field-verified points against a classified raster, with the locational-uncertainty circle, area weighting and both output tables.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path arcpy.jenness.ClassificationAccuracy( in_features=r"D:\data\accuracy.gdb\field_plots", predicted_layer=r"D:\data\accuracy.gdb\veg_classification", observed_field="Field_Class", circle_radius=15.0, linear_units="Meters", weight_by_map=True, map_area_ha=125000.0, out_report=r"D:\data\accuracy_report.txt", out_class_table=r"D:\data\accuracy.gdb\class_stats", out_matrix_table=r"D:\data\accuracy.gdb\error_matrix")
